t65z14_st1p4w2p1: The three grown-up jobs work between people, too. A good peer, someone you take turns listening to as equals, can lend you the Nurturer by staying with you and being warm. And the Protector, by keeping what you say private and sticking to the agreed time. If you say no, they don't push. Your little one might be watching for that. As for your Guide, they don't supply it or decide what your experience means. But a carefully timed question can help you hear your own Guide. They ask without interpreting or giving advice, and leave the answer to you. Then it's their turn.
t65z14_st1p1w2p1: You might tell yourself, "But I'm not dependent on anyone." The words you use in this work direct your attention, though. Unless the painful or negative thing itself needs naming, prefer words that point toward the ability or relationship you want to strengthen. Or toward something you want to do more. Saying "Let's help you build more ways to feel cared for and supported" usually gives your mind a clearer direction than bringing in a label like "dependency" just to deny it or argue with it. In inner-child work and hypnosis especially, make that direction easy to imagine: warmth, protection, steadiness, rest, or whatever's really needed.
t65z14_st1p4w8p1: Some of what the three grown-up jobs do can come from outside you, too. When you take turns listening with a good peer, as equals, their warmth and the way they stay with you lend you the Nurturer for a while. Keeping what you say private, and stopping when the time's up, lends you the Protector. If you say no, they don't push. But they don't act as your Guide, or decide what your experience means. Maybe they're thinking, "Oh, I know what this is about," or "Here's what you should do." They keep it to themselves. A question from them at the right moment can help you hear your own Guide, and what you answer is up to you. Then you trade places.
t65z14_st1p1w1p1: The words you use in this work direct attention. t65z14_ba1p2w7p1: Say they're the one who always remembers your appointments. Over time, reparenting can help you take in some of what they've been doing for you, and start doing it yourself, the calendar part included. What you're after is care your little one can count on from more than one place, while the relationship stays precious and important. Other jobs can go to friends or community, to professionals or services, or to routines and simple tools. Which of these could become more yours? Some are healthiest shared, and some really do belong inside that relationship.
t65z14_ba1p2w6p1: Maybe they're the one who always knows what to cook when you can't think straight. Over time, reparenting can help you pick up some of that and practice it yourself. Not all of it has to land on you or on them, either. Friends and community can carry some, and so can professionals, services, routines and simple tools. What you want is for your little one to feel reliably cared for in more than one way, while the relationship stays as precious and important as it is. So which jobs could become more yours, and which are healthiest shared? A few really do belong inside that relationship.

Don't force a new you to show up just because not knowing feels unbearable. Meanwhile, the grown-up you keeps your routines and protects your body. t65z14_le1w2p2: Missing someone doesn't have to turn into another problem to solve. Sometimes the ache itself can become a cue for love. You're already thinking about them. So don't push the missing away. If love is there, let "I miss you" become "I love you," or offer a simple wish, however you'd say it: "May you be safe. May you be held in love." Picture them, or just feel your care going out to them. It's about what happens in you, so you don't have to believe they receive anything. It doesn't replace grief, contact, boundaries or practical action. If sending love makes you more compulsive or unreal, make it simpler: "I miss you, and I care." Do the same if you can't get back to your life afterward. You can also offer some of the same care to the part of you that's still here.
t65z14_sp6p1w2p1: In the morning, choose one modest intention: "Today I will notice one hook before I act from it." You might already be guessing which one it'll be. It can be any hook, though, whichever one shows up. At night, look back over the day without putting yourself on trial. Where did you notice the hook, and where did it run its whole sequence anyway?
t65z14_lm4p4w3p1: Sometimes care isn't what's missing. The whole horizon of life feels too small. A meal can help, and so can a boundary or a kind sentence, without touching the question underneath: "Why should I want this life at all?" Or however you'd put it. Take that question seriously: what would have to be possible for being alive to feel worth discovering, instead of just something to endure?
t65z14_fg1w2p1: For many people, healing eventually includes some forgiveness, or at least getting out from under active resentment. You can't put it on a schedule, and you don't need it first to be safe or hold someone accountable. If you've been waiting to forgive before setting a boundary, you don't have to. Getting justice and recovering can come before it too. Active resentment can narrow what you see, though, and keep your little one organized around the injury. But pressure to forgive early gets you an enlightened-looking performance ("I'm at peace") while the wound goes underground.
t65z14_fg1w2p3: Understanding them doesn't make what they did harmless, and in theory there were other options. It means punishment can't go back and create the awareness, support or ability they were short on. What's worth doing is repairing what can be repaired, and making a different response more available now. The harm is real, and they're still accountable. Boundaries and legal consequences can still be right, and so can moral judgment and distance, even permanent no-contact. You can understand them and hold them responsible. And yes, you can forgive someone you'll never speak to again. "I understand how you became this way" can sit right beside "I now understand why I shouldn't rely on you for this."
t65z14_fg1w2p4: Forgiving yourself works the same way, and if that's hard, forgiving other people tends to be harder too. Own what you did, and only what was yours. Let the remorse register ("oh no, I really did that"). Repair what you can, by apologizing or making amends. Changing the behavior counts as repair too. Then you're allowed to stop holding yourself hostage, though you're still responsible. Some harms take years to forgive. Forgiving too soon is one trap, and living permanently inside resentment is the other. Don't push it. Over time, keep coming back to how the person became capable of it, until the understanding is real enough to change how you feel.
t65z14_fg1p3w1p1: None of that makes what they did harmless, or means they had no other option in theory. Part of you might want them punished. But punishment can't go back and give them the awareness or support they didn't have enough of. Or the ability. The useful work is repairing what can be repaired, and making a different move more available now. They're still accountable, though, and the harm is real. Boundaries, legal consequences, moral judgment, distance and cutting off contact for good can all still be right. You can understand them and hold them responsible. And forgiving them doesn't mean you ever have to speak to them again. "I understand how you became this way" can sit beside "I now understand why I shouldn't rely on you for this."

If it's someone who hurt you, maybe part of you goes, wait, them too? It isn't asking you to forgive them, or to imagine their childhood. None of this involves contacting anyone. Whether you ever do is a separate decision, and never one to make while you're flooded. All this is so you stop carrying a feeling this many people share, as proof that you alone are defective.

# When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun

Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one life ends and before the next one has formed. A breakup will do it, or moving to another country, an illness, losing your faith or a role, your youngest moving out. So can leaving a family or community, or staying in one on new terms. Tibetan Buddhism calls an in-between state a bardo. You don't have to buy what it teaches about death and rebirth to use the everyday part: endings leave a stretch where the old you is gone and the new one hasn't shown up.

In that stretch, ask what has actually ended, and what you're still trying to keep going. What isn't known yet? What's your little one afraid will happen in the gap? Maybe it thinks it'll always be like this. What practical act or small ritual would mark the ending, without pretending you know the next beginning? Don't force a new you to show up just because not knowing feels unbearable. Meanwhile, the grown-up you keeps your routines and protects your body. Grieve what ended, and stay with your little one while the next life takes shape.

Missing someone doesn't have to turn into another problem to solve. Sometimes the ache itself can become a cue for love. You're already thinking about them. So don't push the missing away. If love is there, let "I miss you" become "I love you," or offer a simple wish, however you'd say it: "May you be safe. May you be held in love." Picture them, or just feel your care going out to them. It's about what happens in you, so you don't have to believe they receive anything. It doesn't replace grief, contact, boundaries or practical action. If sending love makes you more compulsive or unreal, make it simpler: "I miss you, and I care." Do the same if you can't get back to your life afterward. You can also offer some of the same care to the part of you that's still here.
t65z14_secsp7w3:
## Just Like Me

This one works best on a steadier day, when thinking about other people won't pull you out of your own shoes. Name the feeling plainly. Lonely, say. Then think of how many people are feeling that exact thing right now, and wanting it to stop, just like you. Some of them make it worse trying to get away from it. Just like you, sometimes. 😅 Wish all of you, you first, enough support to stay with it, so the pain stops with you.

Breathe however you normally breathe, nothing special. After yourself, wish the same for anyone else who comes to mind. If it's someone who hurt you, maybe part of you goes, wait, them too? It isn't asking you to forgive them, or to imagine their childhood. None of this involves contacting anyone. Whether you ever do is a separate decision, and never one to make while you're flooded. All this is so you stop carrying a feeling this many people share, as proof that you alone are defective.
